articles.title: BJP wins but independents rewrite Rajasthan civic poll math
articles.summary: Rajasthan ULB polls: BJP tops ward tally (4,179) but independents win 2,273, shaping hung civic bodies; BJP wins Jaipur with 78/150.
articles.body: Jaipur: Independents emerged as the decisive force in Rajasthan’s urban local body elections, limiting BJP’s gains and keeping Congress competitive across several towns. BJP finished as the single largest party, but the scale of independent victories turned many civic bodies into arenas for post-poll negotiation rather than clear mandates.According to final figures uploaded on the State Election Commission website, results had been declared in 10,235 of 10,244 wards by late Monday, with BJP winning 4,179, Congress 3,613 and independents picking up 2,273 to collectively take third position and establish themselves as potential kingmakers in urban local bodies where neither major party managed to cross the majority mark.At the urban local body level, BJP secured majorities in four municipal corporations – Jaipur, Bhilwara, Kota and Udaipur – and emerged as the single largest party in Alwar. Of the 47 municipal councils, BJP won a clear majority in 11, Congress in six and independents or others in four. In Fatehpur, Congress was tied with an independent candidate.The results give BJP the numerical edge, but not the sweep it sought in the first major statewide urban electoral test for the Bhajan Lal Sharma govt since it came to power in Dec 2023. Sharma campaigned extensively, holding roadshows in Ajmer, Bhilwara, Udaipur, Pali, Bikaner, Bharatpur, Jaipur, Alwar, Jodhpur and Kota. Even so, the party suffered reverses in key pockets and fell short in several prestige contests.The sharpest setbacks came from politically symbolic terrain.Jhalawar and Baran, former chief minister Vasundhara Raje’s strongholds for four decades, slipped out of BJP’s control. Congress won Jhalawar, while AAP made its political debut in the state by claiming control of its maiden municipal body in Baran.Sharma also faced a difficult verdict in his home turf of Bharatpur despite his direct role in candidate selection. Independents won 36 wards there, compared with 20 for BJP and seven for Congress, leaving the ruling party far from a majority.Pali delivered another blow. BJP lost the city to Congress despite its association with BJP state president Madan Rathore, cabinet minister Joraram Kumawat and former Union minister PP Choudhary.The party also suffered setbacks in parts of Shekhawati and eastern Rajasthan. Its performance in Bikaner and Ajmer, where Congress ended BJP’s 36-year hold over the city, has sharpened concerns within the organisation, particularly with panchayat polls likely later this year.Congress, though behind BJP in the overall tally, gained enough ground to make the point that BJP’s urban dominance remained incomplete. With 2,273 wards, independents are set to influence control in several bodies where neither BJP nor Congress has a clear majority. Their performance points to the continuing strength of local networks, candidate reputation and ward-level grievances over party loyalty in many towns.The State Election Commission Monday postponed, until further orders, elections for chairperson and deputy chairperson in four urban local bodies after technical glitches in EVMs delayed the declaration of results. Results of four wards were withheld after EVMs developed technical snags, leaving counting incomplete.Elections were held in two phases, on Sept 9 and 11, across 309 urban local bodies — 10 municipal corporations, 47 municipal councils and 252 municipalities. articles.title: Husted picks up Steak ‘n Shake endorsement in Ohio Senate race
articles.summary: Steak ‘n Shake has thrown its support behind Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in the toss-up Ohio Senate race — citing his commitment to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement as the fast food company touts its alignment with the Trump administration’s health policies. “We stand with Husted because he champions the #MAHA movement to…
articles.body:
Steak ‘n Shake has thrown its support behind Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in the toss-up Ohio Senate race — citing his commitment to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement as the fast food company touts its alignment with the Trump administration’s health policies.

“We stand with Husted because he champions the #MAHA movement to clean up the American food supply chain and lower the cost for consumers,” the restaurant wrote on the social media platform X Thursday.

The Indiana based chain, which has highlighted its winning record in political endorsements this primary cycle, took a dig at Husted’s opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), for “driving up grocery prices for every Ohio family” through his support of “extreme federal spending.”

Husted is locked in a tight race against Brown, with Cook Political Report and Decision Desk HQ rating the contest as a “toss up.” Brown served in the Senate for nearly two decades, losing his 2024 reelection bid to now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio.)

“Senator Husted is the only candidate fighting to make Ohio healthy, safe, and affordable again. #MAHA,” the fast-food restaurant wrote in response to a video of Husted talking about his food policy stances while standing in front of a Steak ‘n Shake stand.

The burger chain has made a series of moves in recents months in line with the White House’s agenda.

In 2025, Steak ‘n Shake committed to removing all seed oils from their restaurants and switched to only serving cane-sugar Coke-a-cola and grade-A Wisconsin sourced butter following priorities set forth by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The company also appointed a “chief MAHA officer” all in an effort to return fast food to its “glory days.”

Kennedy has sought to reshape nutrition in America since he took over the Department of Health and Human Services, reworking guidelines to follow an “upside down food pyramid” model that prioritizes vegetables, fruits, proteins, dairy and healthy fats at the top and whole grains at the bottom.

“Today, our government declares war on added sugar, highly processed foods loaded with additives, added sugar and excess salt,” Kennedy said at a January press conference.

Husted said in the Thursday video that he is fighting for transparency about the ingredients in food so Americans can “make wise, healthy choices about the food you eat.” The Ohio senator has been vocal about his support for food and nutrition reforms.

“As the executive branch and Congress work together to strengthen a variety of food safety processes, consistent ingredient transparency standards must be part of that conversation,” Husted wrote in a separate post to X in August.

articles.title: Thune: Legislation to regulate AI needs to have a ‘light touch’
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday said any legislation Congress passes to regulate AI must have a “light touch” so as not to stifle innovation and tempered recent warnings that superintelligent AI could exterminate humanity as a “worst-case scenario.” “It needs to strike a balance, light touch. You don’t want to stifle innovation…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday said any legislation Congress passes to regulate AI must have a “light touch” so as not to stifle innovation and tempered recent warnings that superintelligent AI could exterminate humanity as a “worst-case scenario.”

“It needs to strike a balance, light touch. You don’t want to stifle innovation but you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated,” he told reporters.

“Obviously there’s a responsibility for the companies to do that when it comes to the frontier on some of these models,” he added. “There is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of more consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead in the AI race, which I also think is very important.”

Thune made his comments after Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, warned that neither company is acting responsibility and are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

This has fueled fears that superintelligent AI could turn against humanity with devastating consequences, something that Thune on Monday downplayed as a “worst-case scenario.”

“I think there are some of these frontier models … I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI. But there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there and I think that you have to try, like all things, figure out what the realistic approach ought to be,” he said.

“Put guardrails around it, like I said, I think on some of these advanced-risk-type models some guardrails there make sense to me but I think you want to do it in a light-touch way that doesn’t squash innovation,” he added. “We are in a race with China and I think there’s huge upside, obviously, with AI as well. There are a lot of benefits to society along with some risks.”

Thune spoke to reporters after Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called on the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to all senators on the risks posed by AI.

“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way. Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must,” Schumer said in a statement Monday morning.

He said officials need to answer questions about three areas of concern related to AI.

He wants the administration to provide a full accounting of its new framework for testing the most powerful frontier AI models and to detail what it’s doing to prevent AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment from flowing to China.

Schumer said it also needs to explain its plans to defend the United States from increasingly sophisticated AI-enabled cyberattacks.

Trump, meanwhile, has downplayed the dangers and pushed back on calls for more guardrails around AI.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote on Truth Social. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’” he wrote on Truth Social Monday. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

articles.title: Pentagon watchdog says Iran war has led to munitions shortfall
articles.summary: It’s the first public report on the ongoing war started Feb. 28 by the U.S. and Israel.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Defense Department’s inspector general released its first report on the war with Iran on Monday, saying the conflict has resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains as the Trump administration works to replenish weaponry. “To mitigate these constraints,” the report said, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has denied reports that the U.S. is running low on munitions. President Donald Trump said Monday on Truth Social that the U.S. is “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond.” Two weeks ago, Trump posted that the U.S. had “virtually unlimited” amounts of ammunition and lashed out at reports of munitions shortfalls. The congressionally mandated report covers from the start of the war on Feb. 28 through June 30. It is one of the first public accountings from any government agency detailing the cost, scope and scale of the U.S.- and Israel-led conflict to the U.S. military, the State Department and other agencies. It follows reports of low morale among U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East, a depleting stockpile of key munitions and extensive damage to American military and intelligence assets in the region. Among the findings, the report provides one of the first government confirmations that Iran targeted the U.S. Navy’s main logistics hub in the region, in Bahrain, with drones and ballistic missiles. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report. It does not address what was most likely a U.S. strike on an elementary school in Iran during the initial hours of strikes. The military has yet to release an internal investigation into the bombing; NBC News reported in June that a report was being finalized. The watchdog’s report details the damage to military equipment, aircraft and other materiel over the first four months of the war, including the destruction of at least 30 large U.S. drones. It says the war with Iran has cost roughly $33.4 billion, which does not account for repairing damaged facilities. It does include $22.3 billion in expended munitions, $3.7 billion for equipment losses and $7.4 billion in other expenditures. NBC News reported in July that the war had so far cost $80 billion to $100 billion, according to three U.S. officials and three people familiar with the internal cost estimates. The Pentagon publicly said in July that the war cost $37.5 billion. Its estimate does not include the cost of replacing aircraft, repairing U.S. bases and replenishing critical weaponry. Trump initially said the war would last for only weeks. But over the weekend, he said it might not end until “right after” November’s midterm elections or perhaps before. The report also finds that the war has displaced more than 20,000 U.S. military and diplomatic personnel, who were relocated at the outset of the conflict and in the days and weeks after. Most medical evaluations of injured U.S. forces were carried out on the ground, some by local ambulances, and the patients were taken to local treatment facilities because airlift capabilities had been moved because of concerns. And U.S. forces flew as many as 5,000 flights from European bases in support of the war, though Trump has bitterly complained that European allies have not done enough to help support the war. The report catalogs some of the damage to U.S. aircraft and other military gear, as well as some of the American bases in the region. Aircraft costs, for example, include destruction or extensive damage to four F-15E jet fighters, an F-35A Joint Strike Fighter and an A-10 Warthog, which was also destroyed, according to the report. Twelve KC-135 refuelers and nine other aircraft were also destroyed, the report says. More than 30 MQ-9 drones had also been destroyed as of June, according to the report, citing the Congressional Research Service. The State Department sustained more than $208 million in damage in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — according to the report. That includes $184 million in damages to “diplomatic facilities” and $25 million more due to delays in construction projects, the report says. The damage Iran inflicted on U.S. military bases had been far more extensive than is publicly known, NBC News reported in April. Iran also caused more damage to America’s intelligence and surveillance assets in the region than U.S. spy agencies have ever endured, and it is estimated to cost billions to repair, NBC News reported last month. The report does not touch on the morale of U.S. troops who have been deployed as part of the war effort. In recent weeks, concerns about deteriorating conditions for troops serving in the Middle East on the USS Abraham Lincoln during an extended deployment had escalated, and the Pentagon announced it was replacing the aircraft carrier. The Lincoln is en route back to its port in San Diego after a stop in Thailand.

articles.title: Chicago Democratic mayor says he’ll run for reelection
articles.summary: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson (D) announced Sunday he is running for reelection, more than three years after he ascended to the office. “My name is Brandon Johnson, and I am running for reelection in the greatest fricking city in the world, Chicago,” an impassioned Johnson said at a rally, to cheers of “four more years”…
articles.body:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson (D) announced Sunday he is running for reelection, more than three years after he ascended to the office.

“My name is Brandon Johnson, and I am running for reelection in the greatest fricking city in the world, Chicago,” an impassioned Johnson said at a rally, to cheers of “four more years” from attendees.

Johnson, formerly on the Cook County Board of Commissioners, outlasted a crowded field, which included then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot (D), in the nonpartisan mayoral race in 2023.

Voters in the Windy City will head to the polls in February, with a runoff in April if no candidate receives majority support.

The first-term mayor, a staunch progressive, touted his work as mayor on Sunday. The 50-year-old said his “North Star” is working for “the many, and not the few.”

Johnson added, “Real transformation has never come from the top down but from the bottom up.”

Salaries for private industry workers increased by 3.9 percent in the Chicago metro area in June, ahead of the national average of 3.3 percent, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Reports of certain violent crimes have also decreased during Johnson’s tenure. The murder rate, up slightly from last year, is down 33 percent from 2023, according to data from the Chicago Police Department (CPD).

Sexual assaults, robberies and burglaries are down by 10 percent, 53 percent and 25 percent relative to 2023, respectively, while thefts are up by 3 percent, per the CPD data.

But earlier this year, Fitch Ratings downgraded Chicago’s credit rating after Johnson and the city council battled until the 11th hour over a spending plan last December. The impasse stemmed from Johnson’s preference to reinstitute the employer head tax .

Last year, Johnson battled with the Trump administration over its surge of federal immigration officers to Chicago. A recent study from the University of Illinois Chicago’s Great Cities Institute found that the roughly two-month operation cost local businesses more than $1.2 billion last year.

Johnson will have to beat multiple challengers to clinch a second term. Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias (D), Illinois State Comptroller Susana Mendoza (D) and Rep. Mike Quigley (D-Ill.) are among a crowded group vying for Johnson’s office.

articles.title: Trump nominates Wesley Hunt to Saudi Arabia ambassador post
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday nominated Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas) to serve as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia. Trump sent the nominations of Hunt and a slew of other individuals to the Senate, which has to confirm his appointments. The U.S. has not had a full-time ambassador to Saudi Arabia since Michael Ratney left office at…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday nominated Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas) to serve as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia .

Trump sent the nominations of Hunt and a slew of other individuals to the Senate, which has to confirm his appointments.

The U.S. has not had a full-time ambassador to Saudi Arabia since Michael Ratney left office at the end of the Biden administration. Jennifer Larson, a career member of the State Department’s Foreign Service, has led the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on an interim basis since mid-August — succeeding Alison Dilworth.

Hunt is departing the lower chamber after two terms representing Texas’s 38th Congressional District. The 44-year-old former Army officer finished third in the Lone Star State’s Senate GOP primary in March, a race state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) won via runoff over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

The Texas representative is set to leave the House at the end of his term in January. In a statement , Hunt said it was the “honor of a lifetime” for Trump to nominate him to the ambassadorship post.

“Having served in the region both in combat as an Army officer and for two years as a diplomatic liaison in the Kingdom, I understand the strategic importance of the partnership between the United States and Saudi Arabia and the profound responsibility of this position,” Hunt said.

“When confirmed, I will serve with humility and honor, advance his vision of peace through strength and deepen this vital partnership,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to a Hunt spokesperson regarding whether the GOP lawmaker will resign from the House, if confirmed.

Trump and his family have business ties to Saudi Arabia, and the president has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — whom U.S. intelligence said “approved” the 2018 operation that resulted in the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.

Last month, the Trump administration sent a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress. Under the 30-year deal, U.S. companies would be able to develop the kingdom’s civil nuclear infrastructure.

The president has stipulated, though, that Saudi Arabia must normalize ties with Israel for the deal to take effect.

articles.title: Hochul accused of ‘hit job’ on behalf of teachers’ unions in act of ‘pure censorship’: labor group

articles.body: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is being accused of conducting a "hit job" on free speech on behalf of teachers unions after she signed a law giving the state attorney general the power to fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union. Hochul signed a law last week prohibiting people and organizations from using deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union or union representative. The law, which took immediate effect, allows Democratic Attorney General Letitia James to investigate and sue to stop alleged violations, including those involving out-of-state groups. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per incident. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per violation, including against organizations outside New York. Pennsylvania sees third measles-associated death

A coroner in Pennsylvania reported another death tied to the state’s worsening measles outbreak.

The Jefferson County coroner in a release initially posted to Facebook said a woman died Saturday from “ complications associated with measles.” “Out of respect for the privacy of the deceased and her family, no additional identifying information will be released,” the statement added. In an interview with The Washington Post, the coroner — who was elected as a Republican — said the woman was unvaccinated and had contact with another person who had a laboratory-confirmed case of measles. The coroner’s office said it is currently working with the state’s health department. In a statement Monday, the health department said it is in touch with the coroner and “actively conducting its own review of the case and will update the public when that investigation is complete.” In late August, the state’s health department reported two infant deaths that it described as “ measles-associated.”

But Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. criticized the finding and suggested the office of Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) may have fabricated the deaths. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has subsequently refused to count the deaths in its official 2026 tally, citing a lack of standardized definition. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that Pennsylvania officials had not notified the agency of the death as of Sunday night, and that the state has not requested official outbreak support from the agency. Deborah Houry, a former CDC chief medical officer, said states don’t always request outbreak support. Houry, who resigned last year when Schwartz’s predecessor was fired, said it’s also not unusual that Pennsylvania hasn’t yet notified CDC. “It likely shows PA is following the process, ” Houry said in a text message. “The adult death was first reported by the county coroner, and Pennsylvania is conducting its epidemiologic review. Formal notification would appropriately follow that review if the case meets the state definition.” According to the state, a confirmed measles-associated death is a death that occurs within 30 days of symptom onset in an individual with “clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory test and that is not due to unrelated causes (e.g. a motor vehicle accident). ” Additional information, such as whether an individual was exposed to measles prior to their death or supporting medical records, is also considered, the state said. A death would not be determined to be measles-associated if there was no laboratory evidence of measles infection or if the death was determined to be due to other unrelated causes.

articles.title: Trump vowed to identify more of the donors to his ballroom project. That hasn’t happened yet.
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly promised to share the names of the private donors funding his massive ballroom.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly promised to share the names of the private donors funding his massive ballroom. But nearly a year after he tore down the White House’s East Wing to make room for the roughly $400 million project, only a partial list of contributors has been made public. “I’ll give you names,” Trump said in the Oval Office just last month. “In fact, I wanted to put them out today, but we got a little busy.” The White House released in October an initial list of 37 donors whom Trump feted at an East Room dinner event to “Establish the Magnificent White House Ballroom,” an official said at the time. The list included corporations, individuals and family foundations. Among them were Comcast Corp., NBCUniversal’s parent company; Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Lockheed Martin and Coinbase. The White House did not disclose how much each company donated or whether they made additional donations after the initial 2025 dinner. Since then, no additional donors have been made public by the Trump administration, though a few have acknowledged donations on their own, including Nvidia and Vantive Healthcare. Democrats in Congress and government transparency groups have raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest and federal favoritism toward anonymous donors. Trump initially estimated that the ballroom would cost $200 million, paid for entirely by donors, including himself, though it is not clear if he has contributed to the project. Since then, the price tag has risen to at least $400 million, according to the administration’s latest estimate, with additional taxpayer funding going to security improvements for the White House writ large, which could include the ballroom site. The White House declined to comment for this story. The donations are funneled through the Trust for the National Mall, a tax-exempt nonprofit organization which did not respond to a request for comment. Individual and corporate donors can typically deduct the amount they contributed from their federal income taxes. A person raising money for the ballroom told NBC News last year that they were asking for donations of $2.5 million to $5 million and that the deduction is one reason people choose to give. Last month, congressional Democrats pushed for more information about the donors, saying the public has a right to know if entities are making donations to a project Trump has personally prioritized in order to seek benefits from his administration, an indication they will likely probe the project if they win back the House in November’s midterm elections. The House Natural Resources Committee and the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee have requested more information from the National Park Service and Trust for the National Mall. “The Trust may have been used as a vehicle for billionaires and corporations to curry political favor with the Trump administration in a potential violation of federal law,” the lawmakers wrote. Democratic senators, including Sen. Richard Blumenthal, have also pressed the donors directly for more details, as groups like Public Citizen, a progressive consumer rights advocacy group, have raised questions about possible conflicts of interest. Over half of the publicly identified corporate ballroom donors, 14 out of 27, have received new or bigger government contracts since October, totaling over $50 billion, according to Public Citizen’s analysis. The group also found that 16 of the 27 donors are either currently facing federal enforcement actions or have had them suspended by the Trump administration. The president has insisted the ballroom and military complex are essential for national security, a case the Trump administration made to several lower courts before going to the Supreme Court to justify its ongoing construction. In late August, the justices ruled 5-4 to allow it to move forward. Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court’s three liberals in dissent, writing that the plans are “likely unlawful.” Trump has insisted that no taxpayer money is being used for the ballroom, but at least $300 million of Secret Service funds were redirected to the White House for security enhancements to the overall complex, according to Office of Management and Budget documents, which could apply to the ballroom as well. Republicans in May suggested using $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to secure the ballroom project, but that funding did not get off the ground. Trump has continued to make a security case for the ballroom, particularly after a gunman attempted to gain access to the White House Correspondents’ Dinner earlier this year. Such events could take place in a much more secure ballroom on the White House campus in the future, he’s suggested, though the event is independent and hosted by an outside nonprofit of journalists. “The people that are opposing the ballroom are people that, in my opinion, are very disloyal to our country, very, very disloyal to our country,” Trump told reporters last month. The Trump administration says the project is about 65% complete, with 250 crew members working 20 hours a day to get it done. It’s expected to be completed by the summer of 2028. “It’s a gift from great patriots of this country,” Trump said in August.

articles.title: As AI fears spike, Trump bats down calls for regulation
articles.summary: President Trump is downplaying the mounting concerns about artificial intelligence and resisting calls for regulation, putting him out of step with a growing chorus of worries coming from within the tech industry and both sides of the political aisle. Trump, speaking with reporters over the weekend and in social media posts on Monday, said warnings…
articles.body:
President Trump is downplaying the mounting concerns about artificial intelligence and resisting calls for regulation, putting him out of step with a growing chorus of worries coming from within the tech industry and both sides of the political aisle.

Trump, speaking with reporters over the weekend and in social media posts on Monday, said warnings about AI going rogue and endangering humanity were overblown.

“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that … shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said.

The president doubled down on his position in a TruthSocial post on Monday, defending his approach and calling out Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned of the dangers of unchecked AI in a blog post over the weekend.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” the president wrote. In a second post, he called the fear of AI destroying humanity a “hoax.”

Stocks plummeted in response to growing calls for AI regulation on Monday, with the Nasdaq Composite Index falling 0.9 percent and the S&P 500 dropping 0.6 percent.

Industry officials beyond Amodei have also weighed in. OpenAI’s Sam Altman wrote in an X post that the “world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened.”

“We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI,” he wrote.

Elon Musk, one of Trump’s closest allies in the tech world, said, “Dario is right,” in a post on X this weekend.

Trump and his allies argue that less regulation on AI is essential for Washington to win the AI race against Beijing.

“He is very much a trust the plan, trust the system, trust the markets, trust the innovators kind of guy,” said Chris Johnson, a Republican strategist and president of the American Energy Leadership Institute.

“There are two groups of people: there are Americans and panicans, and you don’t want to be a panican,” he said.

But the hands-off approach to AI regulation threatens to open the president up to political blowback as Americans grow increasingly concerned about AI and the data centers that power the technology.

Seventy-eight percent of likely voters said they would choose “mandatory standards” on AI while only eight percent said they chose “no regulation,” according to a poll released in June from the nonpartisan AI Policy Institute.

“I do think that Republicans are going to talk more and more about AI safety and security. The polling data on this is really clear,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican strategist and CEO of the Alliance to Secure AI.

“I see the political winds shifting on this in favor of more regulation, and I’m confident that the White House, the Speaker [Mike Johnson (R-La.)], and [Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-N.D.)] are going to get together with the companies and find some way to move forward to pace development, and to put at least some safeguards on the technology,” he continued.

The warnings come as Congress heads back into session for the final time before November’s midterm elections. Johnson said Monday that the White House will host a meeting with AI executives as soon as this week to “sort this out.”

AI has emerged as a top issue on the campaign trail, with Democrats and Republicans calling for guardrails.

In Michigan, Democratic senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has called for “public oversight” on AI, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R ) has enacted regulations on AI data centers in his own state.

“We are on an exponential growth curve in AI,” Steinhauser said. “This issue is not going to recede.”

“You can see by January or February of next year when the presidential cycle kicks off anyway, you’re going to see every candidate talking about this,” he continued.

Vice President Vance, a leading potential 2028 contender, urged caution on the issue while speaking to reporters on Monday.

“I feel a little bit weird about the fact that we have so many frontier AI tech companies’ kind of talking to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a trojan horse, so I think we just have to be careful about this,” Vance said, noting that there are “risks” and “benefits” to the technology.

Trump and other proponents of AI data centers argue they are essential to the country’s national security and development, while opponents point to the financial and environmental costs.

Doug Kelly, CEO of the tech industry group American Edge Group, which promotes data centers, noted that China leads the U.S. in energy, adoption, and talent for AI, but that the U.S. still holds an advantage in infrastructure and chips.

“We can’t give up our strongest advantage. We need to be able to build more data centers, manufacture more advanced chips, and develop the world’s best AI models here in America,” Kelly said.

Will Rinehard, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the Chinese “are definitely very, very, very closely monitoring what’s happening in America because we have an incredible bench of talent.”

But he said he doesn’t see the implementation of guardrails significantly slowing progress.

The AI guardrail conversation has brought together some unlikely allies. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders (I) and former White House adviser Steve Bannon are set to speak at the same Pro-Human Assembly event on Tuesday to push for human-controlled AI.

Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said “the future will favor a paired approach.”

“National security policies that maximize the U.S. lead over China are essential to ensuring AI doesn’t tip the balance of power against us,” she said. “They also buy time to build a domestic regulatory framework that ensures AI is developed and deployed in ways that are safe and broadly beneficial.”

Others say they see an emerging dividing line between Republicans and Democrats on AI.

“You can always peel off a few people from the other side and find ways to make them sympathetic to your point,” said Johnson of the American Energy Leadership Institute. “I think generally Republicans and conservatives broadly are going to be much more in line with the president.”

“If you’re somebody who’s in the tech industry or in the tech policy space, you need to start waking up real quick to who’s on team red versus who’s on team blue,” he added.

articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said in an interview on Monday that he wouldn’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris ran for a third bid, pointing out that they’d both be fighting over similar bases of supporters.

“First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it,” Newsom told CNN’s Jake Tapper while fly fishing in Montana. “Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good.”

When Tapper offered the counter argument that Harris had won twice and lost while Newsom had never ran before, the California governor argued that they’d split their share of primary voters if the two ran against each other.

“I know her base of supporters. I know her friends,” Newsom said. “The [Venn] diagram on that is just pure crossover.”

“I wouldn’t do that to people,” he added.

Newsom is widely floated as a potential 2028 White House candidate and is mulling a possible run. Harris, who also hails from California and shares a similar political orbit with Newsom, is as well.

The California governor’s interview marks the first time that he’s addressed forgoing a White House bid if his Golden State counterpart were to join the 2028 primary mix.

Many potential hopefuls on either side are expected to start announcing decisions after the November midterms.

Newsom has been traveling to states like South Carolina and Michigan, while Harris has traveled across the country as a part of her book tour while weighing in on the midterm races.

Having two Californians — potentially three, with Rep. Ro Khanna — could be a risky bet for Democrats not only because they would share the same political home, but hailing from the reliably blue state could make it harder to bring in independents or disaffected Republicans.

I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues,” McConnell wrote in a statement Monday. The senator added that his recovery had been “a long and frustrating process,” saying it had been complicated by “lingering effects of childhood polio.” “I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” McConnell added. The senator has been missing from the Senate since mid-June, when he suffered a fall at home and was “briefly unconscious,” according to a July statement. “I must admit, after two years, two decades after dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today,” McConnell joked to reporters while sitting in a wheelchair on Monday. “So I’m glad to see you. McConnell was hospitalized after his June fall and later released to rehabilitation care. At the time, his office released a photo of the senator in a hospital chair alongside his wife, Elaine Chao. His absence, along with a lack of interview appearances in the media, led to rampant speculation and calls from members of the public and Kentucky’s Democratic governor to release proof that he was fit to serve in Congress or otherwise resign. McConnell, 84, in July addressed why it took him so long to disclose the reason for his absence, saying he couldn’t help but hesitate “to share the vulnerability that comes with getting older.” McConnell’s return comes as a farm bill is set for a markup Wednesday in the Senate Agriculture Committee. Republicans hold a slim 12-11 majority in the committee, meaning McConnell’s presence is needed to send bills to the full Senate floor on party-line votes. McConnell, who is retiring at the end of the year, has faced several health issues in the past few years. The senator took a fall during a Senate Leadership Fund dinner in 2023, leading to a hospitalization and a diagnosis of a concussion and a rib fracture. Later that year, McConnell froze mid-sentence while addressing reporters on the Hill on more than one occasion. McConnell was elected to the Senate in 1984. Rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., is the Republican nominee for the senator’s seat in the ruby red state.

articles.title: McConnell returns to Senate to cast first vote since June
articles.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returned to the Senate Monday evening to cast his first vote since June 11 after spending months away from the Capitol recuperating from a fall he suffered at home. articles.body:
Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returned to the Senate Monday evening to cast his first vote since June 11 after spending months away from the Capitol recuperating from a fall he suffered at home.

McConnell’s long absence and the trickle of information from his office about his condition fueled weeks of speculation about his health and whether he would return to the Senate before the end of his term in January.

“After two years, two decades, actually, of dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today. So I’m glad to see you. Time to get back to work, finish the job of this Congress,” McConnell told an assembled group of reporters outside the Senate chamber before casting a vote for Matthew Byrne, a nominee to serve as district judge for the Southern District of Ohio.

An aide pushed McConnell through the historic Ohio Clock Corridor in a wheelchair, where he appeared frail but in good spirits after three months away from his Senate colleagues.

“I’m here to work on the farm bill, it’s important to my state. And as I think you know I have an ongoing interest in NATO and backing up our good friends who are totally in a fight against the Russians,” he added, referring to Ukrainian forces who are grinding away at the front lines after more than four years of combat against invading Russian forces.

“Welcome back!” McConnell said to reporters, who returned to a busy schedule of votes after the five-week August recess.

McConnell was spotted earlier in the afternoon being wheeled out of his Capitol Hill townhouse by an aide and security detail while a crowd assembled on the sidewalk.

In a statement circulated by his office, McConnell said he was “really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues.”

“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100 percent but I’ve assured Leader Thuen that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our conference needs me,” he said.

McConnell return is a big relief to GOP senators as his presence will give them the votes they need to pass the farm bill out of the Agriculture Committee and to advance regular spending bills out of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

The farm bill stalled in the Agriculture Committee last month after Democrats voted along party lines against the legislation because of disagreements over cuts made to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by Republicans in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Republican leaders are reportedly aiming to try again to advance it this week.

McConnell, who is 84, was rushed to the hospital on June 14 after taking a fall at his Washington home.

His office announced he was discharged from the hospital in early August.

articles.title: Ex-Dem insider exposes what Harris told top donors days before Biden dropped out: 'Insulting'
articles.summary: Lindy Li claims Kamala Harris secretly auditioned for wealthy Democratic donors while publicly insisting Joe Biden would stay in the 2024 race.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, believes Kamala Harris was setting herself up to poach Biden’s donors just days before he dropped out of the race — while still telling voters he could win. Li said she threaded that political needle by staying far away from any criticism of Biden. "It was all charade. She was auditioning for Biden's endorsement, and the way that she did it was by imposing a fake rule on her staff to not talk about her ascending to the nomination," Li said in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital. Li’s chronicling of the months leading up to Biden's suspended campaign, which are included in her book, "Unburdened," adds more detail about how even those closest to Biden understood that his campaign would likely come to a grinding halt following his disastrous 2024 debate — and even before it. EX-BIDEN STAFFER BLAMES BIDEN'S 'HUBRIS' FOR THE 'HELLSCAPE THAT WE LIVE IN': REPORT As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris and someone who had achieved a high profile with the Democratic National Committee (DNC), Li worked with both teams to raise campaign contributions. In the wake of the election, Li has gone public with much of her insider knowledge, raising the alarm over just how many figures inside the Democratic Party had seen the writing on the wall but remained silent. She also detailed how others, like Harris, quickly moved to prepare themselves for what would happen next. In Li’s view, Harris prioritized face time with donors she knew could soon back her own bid. "I was on the call; she would host calls with donors and pretend to support Biden and say there's no daylight between Biden and herself. All the while she was auditioning for those very donors," Li said. HARRIS REACHES OUT TO SOCIALIST MAYOR MAMDANI IN LATEST SIGN SHE'S SHORING UP SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE 2028 BID Li recalled how, in one case, Harris addressed donors about Biden’s viability as a candidate two days before Biden bowed out. "It was either on July 19th or July 20th. Actually, I think it was July 19, 2024; Kamala Harris held a call saying that there was no way that Biden would drop out and that she would stick with him until the end. And these were some of the biggest donors in the party," Li recalled. Biden announced that he would no longer pursue reelection on July 21. After Biden’s announcement, Li recalled that Harris moved aggressively within the Democratic camp to shore up support, insinuating that she had some form of Biden’s backing. "She was flattering people left and right. The first 24 hours were a very intensive charm offensive on her part. And that's how she was able to consolidate it so quickly. She flattered people up the wazoo. It made it abundantly clear that Biden had endorsed her. And Biden initially — I don't know if people know this, but he didn't want to endorse her right away. It took him a while." Notably, although Biden would endorse Harris later that same day, he announced he would not pursue reelection, his support of Harris came as a second message, roughly 30 minutes later. Despite the vice president’s efforts to maintain her support of Biden and back his viability, Li recalled that some of those same donors didn’t buy her story, LIBERAL CNN ANCHOR LASHES OUT AT DEMOCRATS' DECEIT AFTER JILL BIDEN'S ADMISSION ABOUT JOE'S DEBATE SHOWING "A lot of us have group chats. And the immediate reaction is what an effing waste of time. What a charade, how fake. Like these are like the wealthiest people in the country saying that. They were very aware they were being lied to, that Biden was clearly not okay and to be told that he was okay when he was clearly incapacitated," Li said. "It was insulting." articles.title: Gavin Newsom says he won't run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris runs
articles.summary: Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper he won't run for president if Kamala Harris enters the 2028 race, citing crossover.
articles.body: Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he won't run for president if former Vice President Kamala Harris throws her hat in the ring. "I don't know if she runs, but we'll see," Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper in an interview released Monday. "But I wouldn't run if she ran." "If she runs, you will not," a surprised Tapper reacted. "Of course not. Why would I?" Newsom responded. "I wouldn't do that to her ... I wouldn't do that to you. I wouldn't waste everyone's time. Who needs that?" HARRIS STOPS IN KEY PRESIDENTIAL PRIMARY STATE AFTER LEAVING DOOR WIDE OPEN TO 2028 RUN Tapper, who was fly-fishing with Newsom in Montana during the exchange, appeared confused by the governor's stance. Newsom suggested spectators would feast on the "mutual-assured destruction" among Democrats competing for the nomination. "I mean, you do whatever you want. I don't care," Tapper told Newsom. "But counterargument would be, like, you know, she had her shot. And you've never run, and she's run twice." "Yeah," Newsom responded. "I mean, that'd be the approach to the campaign, certainly. That'd be the case you'd make. Pretty good one, actually. That's objectively true." NEWSOM'S ATTACK DOG TAUNTS BUTTIGIEG OVER SOUTH CAROLINA VISIT AS 2028 FIGHT HEATS UP HARRIS REACHES OUT TO SOCIALIST MAYOR MAMDANI IN LATEST SIGN SHE'S SHORING UP SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE 2028 BID "But I know what that means. I know her base of supporters. I know her friends. The Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover. I wouldn't do that," he added. Newsom's name has long been discussed as a potential 2028 contender. However, the fellow Californian and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris may have the inside track to remain on the top of the ticket. Harris holds a double-digit lead over Newsom among Democratic hopefuls by a 24.5-13.5% margin, according to the RealClearPolitics average of polls. Nipping at Newsom's heels within a five-point margin are former Biden Transportation Sec. Pete Buttigieg, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff. articles.title: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed says leaders must address ‘unpaid debts’ to Black communities
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Saturday that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities, arguing that leaders have a responsibility to "understand" and "address" them. El-Sayed — who is facing Republican nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races — made the remarks while speaking at a meeting with women faith leaders hosted by the Woman Difference Collaborative in Detroit, according to a video shared by C-SPAN. "When it comes to black communities in Michigan — when it comes to black communities in America — there are unpaid debts that have long since come due that we are unwilling to acknowledge, let alone pay down," El-Sayed said. "And I understand that we need leaders who are going to understand those debts and address them." ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS El-Sayed made the remarks while responding to a question about how he plans to energize Democratic voters who did not support him in the primary. He said his approach is to keep showing up, engaging with voters and emphasizing his record. "But the question for me is, within my power have I done my best?" El-Sayed said. "And I will challenge people to look at my history and say, ‘Yeah, that man hasn’t done everything he could around the problems he says he cares about.'" ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES During his response, El-Sayed highlighted his work on infant and maternal mortality, asthma and lead exposure. He also called for expanding access to capital for small businesses and increasing investment in housing and schools. El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018 before launching his Senate campaign. EL-SAYED’S LIBERAL AGENDA CLASHES WITH MUSLIM VOTERS WHO BACK HIM ANYWAY: ‘MALE VERSION’ OF ILHAN OMAR The Detroit event also featured discussion of El-Sayed's public health record, U.S. aid to Israel, his endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, campaign attack ads from Rogers and criminal justice issues, according to C-SPAN. articles.title: Trump loyalist subpoenaed John Brennan before resignation last week
articles.summary: A Trump loyalist heading a “grand conspiracy” investigation into some of Trump’s grievances signed a subpoena seeking testimony from former CIA director just before his resignation from the Justice Department last week.
articles.body: A Trump loyalist heading a “grand conspiracy” investigation into some of Trump’s grievances signed a subpoena seeking testimony from former CIA director John Brennan just before his resignation from the Justice Department last week, his lawyer told a court Monday. On Sept. 9, Joe diGenova signed the document aimed at Brennan for testimony before a federal grand jury sitting in Fort Pierce, Fla., Brennan attorney Ken Wainstein wrote in a declaration. After Wainstein reached out to diGenova after he accepted the subpoena on Sept. 10, diGenova wrote that he would “arrange counsel” to speak with them. Brennan’s testimony was preliminarily set for Oct. 15. diGenova resigned later in the day on Thursday. On Friday, Wainstein said, 2020 election denier Kurt Olsen — now part of the prosecutorial team in the Southern District of Florida — told Brennan’s team that there were multiple “viable” grand jury investigations into his client “including a ‘far-reaching’ investigation in Fort Pierce that includes ‘issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond’ into whether President Donald Trump had his civil rights violated.” Another investigation is running out of District of Columbia, looking into Brennan’s statements before Congress, Olsen confirmed. “Mr. Olsen explained that Director Brennan was a ‘target’ of the narrower investigation, and the investigation for which he was now being subpoenaed was the ‘more wide-ranging conspiracy,’ as to which our client was a ‘subject.’ However, he explained that the narrower investigation was ‘still viable,’ and that the issues in the narrower investigation might also be part of the larger investigation, such as being overt acts,” Wainstein wrote. The filing came shortly before Wainstein and co-counsel Daniel Gelber appeared in court on Monday before U.S. District Judge Jia M. Cobb in Washington to argue the judge order the Justice Department to preserve communications about the Brennan case. Brennan’s team, citing reports of the Trump administration’s widespread use of Signal to conduct official government business, is seeking an injunction to force the government to preserve communications for a potential future argument that the case is a vindictive prosecution driven by Trump. “Director Brennan seeks nothing more than to ensure that the government does what it is already obliged to do — preserve all records and communications relevant to the government’s preordained decision to investigate and prosecute him,” his team wrote in a filing last month. “The government is not going to disclose what it’s destroying,” Wainstein said in court on Monday. “There’s a lot of really underhanded stuff going on in this investigation.” Wainstein also said the Justice Department had been playing “games” with the case, and said they were “pretty unprecedented example of judge shopping” by running the federal grand jury probe from the courthouse in Fort Pierce in the Southern District of Florida, where Trump-friendly U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon is the sole jurist on the bench. Public officials are operating lawfully and honestly in discharging their official duties and they’re not entitled to regular rules, Wainstein argued. “If anything, it’s a presumption of irregularity,” Wainstein said. Wainstein argued that diGenova’s was the “strongest champion” of a case against Brennan — noting diGenova called Brennan a “traitor” a few years ago — and that his departure sent “a very clear message” about the case. diGenova did not answer a phone call on Monday. Jeremy Newman, an attorney with the Justice Department, argued that the Justice Department conceded that it had a legal obligation to maintain some communications under the Federal Records Act, but that Brennan was making an argument that his constitutional rights were violated, and that he lacked standing to bring the suit given that he had not been charged. If he were charged, Newman said, then he could take those issued up with a judge and seek remedies. Brennan’s team argued that will be too late, because any Signal messages exchanged about the case will have long disappeared by that juncture. Wainstein suggested Justice Department leaders were using disappearing messages because they don’t want “history to know about what they were saying to one another” about what he called a politically-driven investigation. NBC News reported in May that the FBI was conducting interviews with current and former CIA officers as part of the investigation. diGenova told NBC News on Friday that there was a specific event which sparked his departure, but wouldn’t go into details about the matter. “Everybody was in their lane, and then some lanes got crossed, and then I decided to leave,” diGenova told NBC News. After diGenova’s departure, the investigation is being run by U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones with support from Main Justice, according to a person familiar with the matter.

articles.body:
Trump slashes climate rules for coal and gas plants

The Trump administration on Monday gutted regulations that limited planet-warming emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants.

The move allows a sector that makes up a large share of the U.S.’s climate change contributions to release greenhouse gases unchecked by the government. It’s expected to be a win for the fossil fuel industry, while allowing the release of significantly more planet-heating pollution.

When it proposed to kill the regulations entirely last year, the Trump administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, this would result in the release of 123 million more metric tons of carbon dioxide, equivalent to putting an additional 28.7 million gas-powered cars on the road.

Monday’s move could be slightly different . While it is expected to repeal large swaths of Biden-era power plant regulations, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) assistant administrator Aaron Szabo told reporters that limited pieces of Biden- and Obama-era regs would remain in place.

In addition to Monday’s final rule, the EPA proposed to find that the Clean Air Act does not give it the authority to regulate power plant emissions due to their climate impacts. If finalized, Szabo said that this move could block future administrations from regulating power plants’ climate emissions.

articles.title: Trump calls Nvidia CEO to talk AI — and gets put on speakerphone in all-hands meeting
articles.summary: President Donald Trump called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a company all-hands meeting and gave another full-throated defense of artificial intelligence after Huang put the call on speakerphone.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Monday called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a company all-hands meeting and gave another full-throated defense of artificial intelligence after Huang put the call on speakerphone. Trump characterized concerns about AI safety as a “hoax,” while telling Huang that the U.S. had to beat China in AI innovation and development. “The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax,” Trump said, suggesting that critics are “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen. That could be political people, that could also be China.” Trump also lauded politically unpopular data centers, calling them “great” and saying they make people and states “wealthy.” “It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years, it’s bigger than the internet and AI, you know, much more so,” he said, while adding that people “have to be a little careful” and do things “prudently.” A video of Trump’s call, posted on X, was reposted by the Trump War Room account, which is associated with a Trump-aligned PAC. The call is also included in a podcast that Huang was recording at the time. Nvidia said it had no comment on Huang’s exchange with Trump or whether they will be meeting soon to discuss these issues. Trump’s comments to Nvidia, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers of AI chips and hardware, come as AI leaders have called for slowing down development of the technology. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay over the weekend that AI development needed safeguards, which was quickly endorsed by Tesla CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, among others. It came after last week researchers at leading AI companies stepped down from their jobs and spoke out over safety concerns, some describing them as an existential threat to humanity. Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats last week to prioritize the development of an AI agenda. Trump, however, has firmly stood by his support for AI development. In a flurry of social media posts Monday, Trump described AI concerns as a “SICK conspiracy” and a “hoax.” During the Nvidia phone call, Trump said he assumed Huang was on the same page as him regarding AI development; Huang said they were. “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people,” he told Trump during their call. The Nvidia CEO, who helped persuade Trump last year to not send National Guard troops to San Francisco, sits on Trump’s council of science and technology advisers. He has lobbied lawmakers to allow sales of Nvidia around the world, which lawmakers have said could advantage China and undercut U.S. leadership in technology. His conversation with Trump came as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who had been urged by House Democrats to end recess early so the lower chamber could take legislative action regarding AI safety, said this week that industry leaders should be the ones taking the lead on safety. Johnson said Monday that Trump would call a meeting with AI leaders. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News that a meeting between Trump and the leaders was “in the works,” but no clear timing had been nailed down.
